A prairie is a large, open stretch of land that is covered mostly by grasses and wildflowers, with very few trees or sometimes none at all. Think of it as nature's giant green carpet — wide, mostly flat or gently rolling, and stretching as far as the eye can see in every direction. The sky feels enormous above a prairie because nothing tall is blocking your view.
What Makes a Prairie a Prairie?

Three things define a prairie:

Grasses, not trees. The dominant plant life is grass. Not the short grass of a lawn, but wild grasses — some ankle-high, some taller than a human being. Wildflowers grow among the grasses too, dotting the landscape with color. Trees are rare, and where they do appear, it's usually along the banks of a stream or river.

Rich, deep soil. Prairie soil is some of the most fertile on Earth. Over thousands of years, grasses have grown, died, and decomposed, building up thick layers of dark, nutrient-rich soil. This is why much of the world's most productive farmland today sits where prairies once were.

A specific climate. Prairies receive a moderate amount of rainfall — enough to sustain grasses and wildflowers, but not enough to grow dense forests. They also experience wide temperature swings: very hot summers and bitterly cold winters. Wind is a constant companion, sweeping almost unobstructed across the open land.

Prairies are most associated with North America. The Great Plains — a massive region running through the middle of the United States and into Canada — is the world's most famous prairie landscape. States like Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, the Dakotas, and the Canadian provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are classic prairie territory.

However, similar grasslands exist on other continents under different names. In South America, they're called the pampas. In Central Asia and Eastern Europe, they're called the steppe. In Africa, grasslands of a tropical kind are called savannas. But the word "prairie" specifically and most naturally refers to the North American version.

Not all prairies are identical. They differ mainly based on how much rainfall they receive, which directly affects how tall the grasses grow.

Tallgrass prairies receive the most rainfall and are found in the eastern part of the Great Plains, in places like Iowa and Illinois. The grasses here can grow extraordinarily tall — sometimes well above your head, reaching over 2 meters (nearly 7 feet). These prairies once looked like a sea of swaying green waves.

Mixed-grass prairies sit in the middle, geographically and in terms of rainfall. The grasses are medium-height, typically reaching somewhere between your knee and your waist. Kansas and Nebraska are good examples.

Shortgrass prairies are found further west, where the land is drier. Grasses here stay short — only ankle to knee height. Eastern Colorado and Wyoming are typical shortgrass prairie regions.

Prairies are teeming with life, even if the landscape looks simple from a distance.

The most iconic prairie animal is the American bison (commonly called the buffalo). Millions of these massive, shaggy animals once roamed the prairies in enormous herds — herds so large they could take days to pass. Today, bison populations are much smaller, mostly in protected areas.

Prairie dogs are small, burrowing rodents that live in large underground colonies called towns. Despite the name, they are not dogs at all — they got their name from the bark-like sounds they make to warn each other of danger. Their burrows also provide homes for many other animals.

Other prairie wildlife includes pronghorn antelope (the fastest land animal in North America), coyotes, jackrabbits, badgers, rattlesnakes, meadowlarks, hawks, burrowing owls, and countless insects, including bees that are critical for pollinating wildflowers.

Fire is also a natural and important part of prairie life. Prairie fires — started by lightning or, historically, by Indigenous peoples — regularly swept across the land. Rather than destroying the prairie, fire actually maintains it. It kills off any young trees that might try to take root, clears away dead plant material, and releases nutrients back into the soil, allowing grasses to grow back stronger than ever.

For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples of North America — such as the Lakota, Comanche, Cheyenne, and many others — lived on and with the prairie. They hunted bison, used the grasses, and shaped their cultures around the rhythms of this landscape.

When European settlers arrived in the 1800s, they called the prairie the "frontier" — a vast, open, and seemingly endless land. The famous covered wagons (sometimes called "prairie schooners," because they looked like ships sailing across a sea of grass) carried thousands of settlers westward across the prairie.

As settlers arrived, they quickly realized how extraordinarily fertile the prairie soil was. Over the following century, the vast majority of North America's original prairie was plowed under and converted into cropland. Today, it is estimated that less than 4% of the original tallgrass prairie still exists in its natural form, making it one of the most endangered ecosystems on Earth. The prairies that remain are deeply valued by conservationists and ecologists.

If you were standing in the middle of a prairie, here is what you would experience. The land around you would be open and vast, with an enormous sky overhead. The wind would be almost constant, making the grasses ripple and sway in waves. Sounds would carry far — a meadowlark's song, the rustle of grass, the distant call of a hawk. In summer, the air might smell of dry earth and wildflowers. In winter, the same open land could feel bitterly exposed, with cold winds sweeping across with nothing to slow them down.

There's a particular kind of beauty to prairies that takes time to appreciate. They don't have dramatic mountains or dense forests. Their beauty is in their scale, their openness, their subtlety — the way the light changes across the grass, the sky that seems to go on forever, and the sense that you are standing in the middle of something ancient and alive.

You'll often see "prairie" used as a describing word (modifier) in compound terms:

Prairie dog — the burrowing rodent described above.
Prairie chicken — a type of wild bird native to grasslands.
Prairie fire — a wildfire spreading across open grassland.
Prairie wind — the persistent, sweeping wind characteristic of open prairie land.
Prairie schooner — a historical term for the covered wagons used by settlers.
On the prairie — a phrase meaning out in the open grassland, often evoking a sense of remoteness or frontier life.

It helps to understand what a prairie is not, by comparing it to similar-sounding concepts.

A meadow is a small, grassy open area, often surrounded by trees or forest. A meadow fits in a field; a prairie stretches for hundreds of miles. A meadow is local; a prairie is regional or continental in scale.

A plain (or "the plains") is a broader geographic term for any large, flat area of land. All prairies are plains, but not all plains are prairies — a plain could be desert, tundra, or farmland.

A savanna is a tropical grassland with scattered trees, found mainly in Africa and parts of South America. Unlike a prairie, a savanna has many more trees spread throughout it, and it exists in a hot, tropical climate year-round.

A steppe is the Eurasian equivalent of a prairie — a vast, dry, temperate grassland found across Russia, Central Asia, and Eastern Europe. It tends to be slightly drier and less biodiverse than a North American prairie.

A prairie is not just a pretty landscape — it is a complete ecosystem, meaning it is a finely balanced, interconnected web of life. The grasses feed the insects, the insects feed the birds, the grasses shelter the burrowing animals, the burrowing animals aerate the soil, the fires clear the old growth, and the rich soil feeds the grasses again. Remove one piece, and the rest is affected. This is why the loss of so much of the world's original prairie is considered a significant ecological crisis, and why efforts to restore and protect remaining prairies are so important.

In short: a prairie is one of Earth's great natural landscapes — wide, grassy, windswept, ancient, and far more alive and complex than it first appears.
